To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the retroviral Rev response element (RRE) is capable of inducing the formation of a unique subcellular compartment that is distinct from the nucleus and that the hepadnaviral epsilon element (ε) can induce mRNA subcellular localization to a distinct subcellular domain that is not nuclear.

the cis-acting RNA structures of retroviruses (RRE and Rev response element, RRE/RRE) and hepadnavirus (enhancer II, E2) exhibit unique subcellular trafficking and gene expression behaviors that are dependent upon the RNA structural element and cellular localization of the RNA.

the cis-acting RNA elements of retroviruses (e.g., HIV-1) and hepadnavirus (e.g., HBV) exhibit diverse subcellular trafficking patterns and that the subcellular trafficking of cis-acting elements is correlated with the expression of viral genes in single infected cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the synthesis and trafficking of RNA molecules in mammalian cells.
the molecular mechanisms of RNA trafficking and gene expression in mammalian cells.
the molecular mechanisms of viral gene expression and replication, and the regulation of these processes in the host cell.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the viral RNA elements studied here have diverse and unique activities that are dependent on the cell type and the RNA element.

cis-acting RNA elements are not only capable of regulating mRNA localization and gene expression, but also that these elements are highly diverse and capable of regulating mRNA subcellular localization and gene expression in a variety of unique and novel ways.
the cis-acting RNA elements are involved in the control of mRNA subcellular localization, which in turn regulates the expression of viral and cellular genes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have discovered that the cis-acting RNA elements from different viruses can be used as a platform to study the diverse and unique subcellular mRNA trafficking behavior of the RNA elements, which can be further used as a model to study the diverse subcellular mRNA transport and localization of cellular genes.

the cis-acting RNA elements from retroviruses (e.g. gag and pol ) and hepadnavirus (e.g. pgRNA ) exhibit diverse mRNA localization behaviors, including nuclear localization, nuclear exclusion, and cytoplasmic localization.
cis-acting RNA elements from different viruses exhibit unique subcellular trafficking and gene expression patterns, which can be recapitulated in a single-cell imaging system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RNA structure is not only important for viral replication but is also important for viral gene regulation.

cis-acting RNA elements can be used to study subcellular mRNA trafficking in real time and that this approach can reveal unexpected, complex, and diverse trafficking behaviors that are intrinsic to these cis-acting RNA structures.
RNA structural elements, which are often thought of as simple, static elements, can have complex behaviors in cells.
